newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Plessey mulls rebasing research, development.
newsitem.headline: Plessey mulls rebasing research, development.

text.p: Plessey Corp Ltd was considering moving some of its technologiocal development to countries that provided stronger support for research and development, chairman Boetie van Zyl said on Thursday.

Speaking at the telecommunications equipment group's annual general meeting, Van Zyl said that although South Africa had a stronger infrastructure than many other developing countries, it did not provide the same support for research and development.
"We have to seriously consider the options of relocating some technological development to countries more favourably disposed to research and development," Van Zyl said.
For example, he said, Malaysia had a scheme through which it paid 100 percent of the development cost of certain new technological products over five years.
This was then backed up by a 10 year tax holiday on profits made on that product.
"Furthermore, there is an import tariff protection of 25 percent plus a surcharge of 10 percent levied to protect the home developed product," Van Zyl said.

"Singapore, one of the nations with the highest per capita income, is looking at ways to modify their education system to encourage original thought and creative thinking to help them to take a lead in the development of new prodcts.
"Government will have to address this issue if we hope to uplift and improve the standard of living of all South Africans."

Chief executive John Temple told Reuters that Plessey could not, in the interests of its shareholders, continue to spend between 30 and 40 million rand a year on research and development and not receive any support from government.
The concept of tariff protection was controversial but it would add to South Africa's technological base both in terms of products and skills.
Temple said that the Department of Trade and Industry was "extremely sympathetic" to Plessey's argument, but had not developed any support programme yet.
"They might still do something, but it might come too late," he said.
